Beállítom One week ago, the Danube's water level in Budapest surpassed its all-time low; at that time, the National Water Management Authority (Országos Vízügyi Igazgatóság) measured the water level at just 30 centimeters (which, of course, does not mean there was only 30 centimeters of water in the river, but rather that this was the level relative to the zero point on the water gauge). The situation has not improved since then; in fact, according to the latest data , the reading was 20 centimeters at 7 a.m. on August 5—which, despite being a slight improvement compared to Monday morning’s measurements, does little to alleviate the problem. If those walking across the Szabadság Bridge during this period look down at the severely depleted river, they’ll be greeted by an interesting sight: the remains of the former Ferenc József Bridge are now visible in the river. This bridge was the predecessor to today’s Szabadság Bridge, and was blown up by the German forces during World War II (or was it? More on that a bit later). Although the Soviets cleared away most of the rubble toward the end of the war, a few pieces of the bridge were left at the bottom of the Danube, parallel to the current bridge. This is not the first time the remains of the old bridge have become visible: the water level of the Danube was very low in 2018 as well—though not as low as now-the lowest point then was 32 centimeters, but the remains of the Franz Joseph Bridge could still be seen emerging from the water. At the time of its construction, this was Budapest’s third bridge; the Art Nouveau style structure was completed in 1896 as part of the Millennium World Fair and was adorned with turuls (a Hungarian mythical bird) and the Hungarian coat of arms. It was named after Emperor Franz Joseph, who also inaugurated it and personally hammered the final silver nail into the structure. The bridgehead of the Franz Joseph bridge on the Buda side in 1926 – Photo: Brúnó Pesti / Fortepan The bridge was blown up in January 1945, 49 years after its construction. The popular belief is that it was destroyed by retreating German troops, but historian Krisztián Ungváry says that this is not at all certain; this may have been the narrative pushed by postwar Hungarian and Soviet propaganda, given that the Soviet military leadership also had an interest in having the bridge blown up—so much so that Stalin himself actually issued the order for the destruction of the Budapest bridges. At 10:15 p.m. on January 16, the 9th SS Mountain Corps sent a telegram stating that the Franz Joseph Bridge had been destroyed in a bombing raid. Previous attacks had already damaged its deck, but crossing still remained possible. The bridge was ultimately destroyed because a Soviet mortar shell—not an aerial bomb—triggered the explosive charge previously installed on it by German troops. The blown-up bridge in 1945 – Photo: Fortepan The river swallowed up almost the entire central span, with the riverbank abutments also sustaining damage. The war was still raging when the Soviets started dismantling the unusable remains of the structure and built a pontoon bridge on top of the ruins. This was destroyed by drifting ice in January 1945. When the construction of the new Szabadság Bridge started, they used the remaining, still usable structural elements of the previous bridge. This ended up being the first bridge to be rebuilt across the Danube after World War II. Work began in the summer of 1946, and the bridge was opened to the public on August 20 of the same year. The so-called Rock of Poverty is actually located quite close to today’s Szabadság Bridge; This rock only becomes visible when the Danube’s water level is very low—hence its name. It may be that the remains of the Ferenc József Bridge will soon be added to the list of landmarks signaling drought. The rebuilt and renamed bridge at its dedication ceremony on August 20, 1946 – Photo: Gara family / Fortepan It’s worth mentioning that the part of Gellért Hill facing the Danube today is the result of human intervention; in the past, the river stretched all the way to the base of the cliffs and kept eroding the unstable hillside. According to the Dunai Szigetek blog , landslides were quite common, and as a result, huge boulders would end up scattered across the riverbed. One of these cliffs is the Ínség Cliff, but there are plenty more: one of them, a roughly 60-meter-long rocky ridge located to the southwest of Szabadság Bridge has a visible impact on the river’s flow patterns. If one looks out from the bridge in that direction, one can often see the funnels of massive whirlpools here. The remnants of the Ferenc József Bridge have been examined using sonar , and the images clearly show the location of the pile of debris relative to the Szabadság Bridge. A significant portion of the wreckage is now covered up by a layer of sediment, but a small part still protrudes from the river’s sludge, offering a great photo opportunity for anyone passing by. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/the-poli.text: The political crisis, in it’s sixth month. Sorin Grindeanu demands restoration of majority with the Liberals and UDMR „Romania could already have had a government with full powers, capable of changing the country’s economic direction, if restoring a stable majority had been put before political and electoral calculations,” Grindeanu claims. „Five months of gridlock have passed and we are once again faced with the same choice: do we put people, the economy and Romania’s interests first, or are we still looking for political formulas that only solve the problem of installing a Government? PSD supports the restoration of a stable majority alongside PNL and UDMR and is ready to assume the responsibility of governing. All based on a program that would give Romania the chance to recover its economic course, to protect the purchasing power of Romanians, and to massively stimulate investments to create jobs. A discussion about the future of a country cannot be reduced to just the number of votes needed to install a Government. We must also talk about what happens after the inauguration, about the ability to make decisions and see them through. „When almost 90% of Romanians said that the country is going in the wrong direction, all parties that received their vote to represent them in Parliament have a duty to take this signal into account and respond through concrete decisions, not just through political declarations,” Sorin Grindeanu said. The message comes in the midst of a political crisis The government led by Ilie Bolojan was dismissed by a motion of no confidence on May 5. President Nicușor Dan appointed on October 5 diplomat Luca Niculescu , secretary of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the fourth nomination for the position of prime minister in this crisis. After the appointment, Grindeanu stated that the new nomination „continues to defy parliamentary mathematics.” UDMR announced that it could vote for Niculescu, provided that there were no negotiations with AUR and SOS Romania, PNL said it would decide after analyzing the program and the list of ministers, and AUR announced that it would not give him any votes. According to some political sources, the inauguration vote could take place on October 19. Read more: • A 15 year old student injured two classmates in Pitesti high school. Greece: 14,000 march in Athens against rising living costs Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 25 November 2026 - 19:20 GMT+1 Thousands demonstrated across Greece on Wednesday 25 November 2026 during a 24-hour strike against rising living costs and stagnant wages. The industrial action disrupted metro services, grounded flights and kept ferries in port. … More Around 14,000 people took to the streets of Athens and Thessaloniki , according to police, in response to strike calls by unions representing civil servants, dockworkers and teachers. In the capital, demonstrators carrying banners and red flags gathered outside the Greek parliament , chanting slogans under the watch of riot police. The industrial action disrupted Athens metro services , kept ferries in port and grounded flights to and from 15 regional airports . Workers, students and pensioners demanded higher wages, better working conditions and improved public services as rising living costs continued to erode their purchasing power. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Although Greece's economy is forecast to grow by 1.8% this year, outpacing the eurozone average of 1.1% , many households are struggling to make ends meet. The gross monthly minimum wage stands at €968 , while housing costs and rents have soared in the wake of the post-pandemic tourism boom. Annual inflation reached 5.7% in October , according to the national statistics authority, Elstat . The civil servants' union ADEDY condemned stagnant wages, energy insecurity and deteriorating public healthcare and education services. Conservative prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis , who is seeking a third term in next year's election, has pledged to raise the minimum wage to €1,000 in early 2028 if re-elected.
